claims.text: A conventional Cr–Mo low-alloy steel with controlled impurity levels will display a ductile–brittle–ductile transition after suitable tempering treatments.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition is driven by temper embrittlement.
Phosphorus or tin can segregate to grain boundaries in Cr–Mo low-alloy steel during tempering.
Impurity segregation occurs preferentially within an intermediate tempering-temperature window.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation weakens intergranular cohesion.
Weakened intergranular cohesion causes a pronounced reduction in ductility.
At lower tempering temperatures, impurity diffusion is too slow to produce significant grain-boundary segregation.
At higher temperatures, grain boundaries are less affected by impurity segregation.
Higher thermal energy dilutes the mechanical effects of grain-boundary segregation and restores ductility.
Ductility will decrease significantly within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
Impact toughness will decrease significantly within the same narrow intermediate-temperature window.
Ductility will be higher both below and above the embrittlement window.
High-entropy and other compositionally complex alloys do not exhibit temper embrittlement characterized by a narrow-window dramatic ductility loss.
The magnitude of the embrittlement effect depends on impurity content.
The magnitude and temperature range of embrittlement depend on processing history and heat-treatment parameters.
Cr–Mo steel with minimal impurity content may not show a pronounced ductile–brittle–ductile transition.

contradictions.description: The causal temperature window is attributed to tempering temperature in the intervention and mechanism, but the conditions and experimental design also describe spanning low, intermediate, and high mechanical-testing temperatures. This conflates heat-treatment temperature with test temperature, leaving unclear which variable is expected to produce the ductile–brittle–ductile sequence.
